passage:
Saturday, 11 pm
Watched another video tonight: a guy who dropped out of college at nineteen and now owns a whole company. Three different toppers on the news said they only studied four hours a day. And that streamer everyone follows quit school in Class 11. So clearly school is optional if you're good.
I told Asif I might skip the coaching classes and just build my baking page instead. He said, "You only hear about the ones who made it." Classic Asif, always the wet blanket.
But... I tried to think of one person I actually know who left school and got famous. I couldn't. I only know them from videos.
Anyway. Sleeping on it.
Irawati

qa.q: What did Irawati tell Asif about the coaching classes?
qa.a: Irawati told Asif about maybe skipping the coaching classes to build a baking page instead.

qa.q: Why does school seem optional to Irawati tonight?
qa.a: Irawati feels hopeful and excited because every story on screen is someone who dropped out and succeeded, so the path looks easy and the many who failed never appear.

qa.q: What could Irawati do before deciding about the coaching classes?
qa.a: Irawati could look for people who tried the same path and didn't make it, and keep the classes while testing the baking page on the side.

qa.q: How does Asif see the videos Irawati is watching?
qa.a: Asif thinks they only show the ones who made it, so they give a false picture of how easy the path is.

grounding: A teenager concludes school is optional after seeing only dropouts who succeeded, missing the many who failed.

passage: Every time Suresh anna came home to Kothapalli from the city, he arrived in a new car and handed out sweets at the bus stand. Everyone knew he'd left school in Class 9. Darshan, fifteen, watched him from the tea shop and made up his mind. "School is a waste," he told his sister Urmila that night, while she checked his notebook by the light of the lantern. "Suresh anna left, and look at him." Urmila put the notebook down. "And Ramu? And the two Reddy boys? They left too." Darshan shrugged. He hadn't thought about them; nobody talked about them. Ramu worked at the brick kiln now. The Reddy boys had gone to the city and come back with nothing, and they never stood at the bus stand handing out sweets.

qa.q: What did Suresh anna do every time he came home?
qa.a: He arrived in a new car and handed out sweets at the bus stand.

qa.q: Why did Darshan decide school is a waste?
qa.a: Darshan felt impressed by Suresh anna's new car and sweets at the bus stand, while those who left and struggled were never talked about.

qa.q: What could Darshan ask before deciding to leave school?
qa.a: He could ask what happened to everyone who left, like Ramu and the Reddy boys, not just the one who came back rich.

qa.q: How does Urmila see Suresh anna's story differently?
qa.a: Urmila remembers Ramu and the Reddy boys too, so she sees Suresh anna as one success among several who struggled.

grounding: A village teenager decides school is pointless from one visible success, not seeing the dropouts who quietly failed.

passage:
Noa had watched the video three times on the bus home in Haifa: a famous chef who'd left school at fifteen and now owned restaurants in four countries. Then another: a singer who never finished school. Then a tech founder who'd dropped out.
At dinner she announced, "I'm leaving school after this year to cook. School is a waste. Look at them, they all made it."
Her older brother Hiroshi, visiting from university, set down his fork. "How many people left school to cook and didn't end up in a video?"
"I don't know. That's not the point."
"It's exactly the point. Nobody films the ones who didn't make it."
Noa scrolled faster, showing him more faces, all smiling, all successful. The more she scrolled, the surer she felt. It didn't occur to her that the screen only ever showed the winners.

qa.q: How many countries did the famous chef own restaurants in?
qa.a: The chef owned restaurants in four countries.

qa.q: Why did Noa feel surer the more she scrolled?
qa.a: Every smiling, successful face made leaving school look like a path that always works, so Noa felt more confident and excited, never thinking about the people who never appear in videos.

qa.q: What question from Hiroshi could Noa use as a turning point before deciding?
qa.a: She could try to find out how many people left school to cook and didn't make it, so her choice rests on the whole picture, not only the winners.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi feel watching Noa scroll faster?
qa.a: Hiroshi seems worried and a bit frustrated, since his point about the unseen failures isn't landing and his sister is getting more certain.

grounding: It shows a teenager seeing only successful dropouts and concluding the path is easy, never seeing the many who tried and failed.

passage:
The auditorium at St. Paul's in Aizawl was packed for the careers day talk. The guest, a well-known travel vlogger, told the students he'd failed Class 12 twice. "Marks don't matter. Follow your passion and the money comes." The whole hall cheered.
Lalremsiami, sixteen, clapped hardest. On the walk back to the hostel she said to Shalini, "See? I've been wasting my time on biology. He made it without any of this."
Shalini frowned. "My cousin tried vlogging for three years. Nobody's heard of her."
"She probably didn't try hard enough."
"And the others who didn't make it? They don't get invited to give talks."
Lalremsiami wasn't listening. She was already picturing herself on the stage, the hall cheering for her. That night she left her biology notes in her locker and watched travel videos until the warden switched off the lights.

qa.q: How many times had the guest failed Class 12?
qa.a: He'd failed Class 12 twice.

qa.q: Why did the talk make leaving biology aside feel sensible to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: She saw one successful person who skipped studies and felt it proved the path was easy, and she pictured herself cheered on stage, so doubts felt unimportant.

qa.q: What would you advise Lalremsiami to ask before deciding marks don't matter?
qa.a: Ask how many people tried the same path and didn't get invited to give talks, like Shalini's cousin, before putting away the biology notes.

qa.q: How does Shalini see the vlogger's talk differently?
qa.a: Shalini thinks of her cousin who tried for three years and was never heard of, so the talk looks to Shalini like just one visible winner among many unseen tries.

grounding: It shows a teenager hearing one successful dropout and concluding the path is easy, without seeing the many who tried and quietly failed.

passage:
Monday. Saurabh watched a video about three famous creators who had dropped out of school at sixteen and "never looked back." By bedtime he had told his mother he wanted to quit after Class 10 and make videos full-time. "They did it. It's easy if you're serious."
Wednesday. His aunt Sangeeta, who worked at a media company, came for dinner. "How many kids do you think tried the same thing that year?" she asked. Saurabh shrugged. "Those three made it." "We get two hundred applications a month from young creators," she said. "Most have under a hundred followers after two years. You never see them, because nobody makes videos about them."
Saturday. Saurabh looked up the channels of people who had started when those three did. Most had stopped posting. He didn't delete his camera app. But he did pick up his Class 10 timetable again.

qa.q: How many applications a month does Sangeeta's company get from young creators?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: Why did quitting school seem easy to Saurabh on Monday?
qa.a: He felt inspired and excited by three success stories, never seeing the many who tried and quietly failed.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do on Saturday, and why was it useful?
qa.a: He looked up others who started at the same time and saw most had stopped, which showed him the missing failures.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's mother have felt on Monday night?
qa.a: She was probably worried and alarmed to hear him plan to quit after Class 10 because of one video.

grounding: Over a week, a teenage boy decides dropping out is easy after seeing three success stories, until he looks for those who failed.

passage: Kunal, you say the cricketers on TV skipped studies and did fine, so you can too? Let your Wasim uncle tell you about my own sixteenth year. Our town had one boy, Irshad, who had played for the state team. Everyone talked about him. He had left school after Class 9. So I decided the same path would work for me. I skipped exams to practise at the maidan every day. What I didn't see were the thirty other boys at that maidan who had made the same choice over the years. They weren't on TV. They were driving autos, working in shops, some still bitter. I only found out when our coach, old Hameed sir, sat me down and named them one by one. That evening I went to my teacher and asked for the missed papers.

qa.q: After which class did Irshad leave school?
qa.a: After Class 9.

qa.q: Why did young Wasim believe skipping exams would work?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and inspired by Irshad, the only one everyone talked about, and never saw the boys for whom it didn't work.

qa.q: What turning point changed Wasim's path?
qa.a: Hameed sir naming the thirty other boys one by one, after which Wasim asked his teacher for the missed papers.

qa.q: Why might Hameed sir have named the boys one by one?
qa.a: He probably cared about Wasim and knew that real, familiar faces would make the missing failures impossible to ignore.

grounding: An uncle recalls believing, at sixteen, that skipping school for cricket was a sure path because he only saw the one who made it.

passage: The stream-change form was due at 9 a.m., and at 10 p.m. the power went out across the colony. By phone light, Himani showed Thomas the magazine: "Ten founders under thirty who left school early." "See? They skipped all this and built companies. I'm dropping science tomorrow." Thomas, her classmate from the flat below, scrolled on his own phone in the dark. "Okay, but how many people left school to start a company and didn't make a magazine?" "Nobody knows that." "Exactly. Nobody writes that list." He found an article about the hundreds of start-ups that close in their first year. Himani read it by the flickering screen. At 8:40 the next morning she was still in the science stream, with a new notebook titled "Company ideas, weekends only."

qa.a: At 9 a.m.

qa.q: Why did dropping science feel like a good idea to Himani?
qa.a: She felt excited and inspired by ten founders who left school, not seeing the many who tried and never made a magazine.

qa.q: What did Thomas's question do for Himani?
qa.a: Asking how many didn't make the magazine pointed her to the missing failures, so she kept science and planned her ideas for weekends.

qa.q: What was it like for Thomas to argue by phone light?
qa.a: Thomas seemed calm and caring, gently pointing her to the missing list instead of mocking her idea.

grounding: Under a deadline, a teenage girl nearly drops a subject after reading about founders who left school, until a friend asks about those who failed.

passage: Bhavna's phone was full of them: the girl from Nagpur who left school at fifteen and now had two million followers, the boy who failed Class 12 and built a sneaker brand. Every video ended the same way: "School is a waste. Just start." One evening in their Andheri flat Bhavna told her elder sister Sarika she wanted to drop out after Class 10 and make videos full time. "Look how easy it is. They all made it." Sarika put down her laptop. "How many people do you think tried the same thing?" Bhavna shrugged. "I don't know. These people did it." "The ones who didn't make it don't make videos about it," Sarika said. "You're only seeing the winners. Where are the thousands who quit and are stuck?" Bhavna opened her mouth, then scrolled her feed again, slower this time.

qa.q: What did every video on Bhavna's phone end with?
qa.a: School is a waste. Just start.

qa.q: Why did dropping out seem so easy to Bhavna?
qa.a: She felt excited and inspired because every video she saw showed someone who had made it, so success seemed normal and certain.

qa.q: What question could Bhavna ask whenever she sees a success story?
qa.a: How many people tried the same thing and didn't make it, since the ones who failed rarely post videos.

qa.q: How does Sarika see the videos Bhavna shows her?
qa.a: Sarika sees them as a small, visible slice of winners, hiding the many who quit and are stuck.

grounding: Shows a teenager seeing only dropouts who succeeded and concluding the path is easy, until her sister asks about those who failed.

"Karthik, I'm not doing engineering. I'm going to start a company straight after Class 12."
"Since when?"

"You only read about the ones who made it. It's like looking at lottery winners and saying tickets are a great plan."

passage: The summer I turned sixteen, I was sure I'd skip college and become a playback singer. I'm Jahnavi, and my phone was full of reality-show winners from small towns, all saying, "I followed my dream, and look at me now." It looked simple: audition, get noticed, sing for films. My Rekha Mami was the one who stopped me, gently. She'd auditioned for four shows in her twenties. "Do you know how many girls were in my queue in Hyderabad?" she asked. "Three thousand. Two got through. The rest of us went home and nobody filmed us." I hadn't thought about the queue at all. Only the winners were on my screen. I still sing, and I still audition. But I also enrolled in college, and I stopped thinking the path was easy.

qa.q: How many girls were in Rekha Mami's audition queue in Hyderabad?
qa.a: Three thousand, and two got through.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling that summer about becoming a singer?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt certain and excited, because the winners on the screen made the path look simple.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi change after the talk with Rekha Mami, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Jahnavi kept singing and auditioning but also enrolled in college, keeping the dream while seeing how many never make it.

qa.q: What was the audition like for the people who went home?
qa.a: For the thousands who didn't get through, it probably meant quiet disappointment, with nobody filming or telling their stories.

grounding: A teenager looks back on thinking a singing career was easy because only winners were visible, until an aunt described the unseen queue.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 11

Ritu told me today she wants to leave school after Class 11 to become a full-time content creator. She showed me three videos of creators who dropped out and now "earn crores". "If they could, so can I. It's easy."

I didn't dismiss her. I asked, "How many people do you think tried the same thing and didn't make it?"

She hadn't thought about it. Those people don't make videos about failing.

We looked together at a small study the school counsellor had shared: of hundreds of young creators who started full time, only a handful earned enough to live on. Most quietly returned to studies or other jobs.

Ritu went quiet. She said, "I only ever see the ones who made it."

I suggested she keep creating on weekends, finish school, and talk to her parents and the counsellor together.

Aparna

qa.q: How many videos of creators did Ritu show?
qa.a: She showed me three videos of creators who dropped out.

qa.q: Why did Ritu think becoming a creator would be easy?
qa.a: Ritu felt hopeful and excited because she only saw the few creators who succeeded, never the many who quietly failed.

qa.q: What did Aparna do that helped Ritu see the whole picture?
qa.a: Aparna asked how many tried and failed, and showed data on young creators, without dismissing Ritu's dream.

qa.q: How might Ritu's parents feel talking with the counsellor?
qa.a: Ritu's parents might feel relieved that she's thinking carefully and still being supported in her interest.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager who sees only successful dropout creators and thinks the path is easy.

passage:
Thursday

Passed the huge coaching centre billboard again today. Twenty smiling faces: "Our IIT toppers!" I stared at it the whole bus ride.

I told Kiran, "If I join that centre, I'll get into IIT too. Look, twenty people did it."

Kiran asked, "How many joined that centre?"

I didn't know. Kiran looked it up on the centre's own website. Two thousand students last year.

Twenty out of two thousand.

That's one in a hundred. And the billboard doesn't show the other nineteen hundred and eighty. They're not smiling on any billboard. They're just... gone from the picture.

I'm not saying don't try. I still want to. But I thought it was easy because I only saw the winners.

Going to talk to Amma about it this weekend.

Lakshmi

qa.q: How many students joined the coaching centre last year?
qa.a: Two thousand students last year.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel after hearing the numbers?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt surprised and more thoughtful, realising the billboard only showed the winners.

qa.q: What question from Kiran helped, and why?
qa.a: Kiran asked how many joined the centre, which revealed the many who didn't succeed and aren't shown.

qa.q: How might Amma respond when Lakshmi talks to her?
qa.a: Amma might feel proud that Lakshmi is thinking carefully and help weigh the options.

grounding: A teenager sees only coaching-centre toppers on a billboard and thinks the path is easy, until a friend asks how many joined.
